question: Should I Hire a Fractional CRO If My Sales and Customer Success Teams Do Not Talk?
body:
## Direct Answer

Yes, in most cases a fractional CRO is one of the fastest, lowest-risk ways to fix a sales and customer success divide, because the root problem is rarely the two teams themselves — it is the absence of a single revenue owner who is accountable for the full customer lifecycle. A fractional Chief Revenue Officer gives you that owner on a part-time, lower-cost basis, and the misalignment you are describing is exactly the class of problem the role was invented to solve. That said, hire one only if you are willing to give them real authority over both functions; a fractional CRO with no mandate becomes an expensive mediator instead of a fixer.

When your sales team and your customer success (CS) team do not talk, revenue leaks in the quiet places between them — bad-fit deals get closed, handoffs drop, renewals surprise you, and expansion never happens because nobody owns the whole arc from prospect to renewal. This essay walks through when a fractional CRO is the right instrument, when it is the wrong one, what the engagement should actually produce, and how to structure it so the alignment survives after they leave.

## What does a fractional CRO actually do to fix sales and CS misalignment?

A fractional CRO is an experienced revenue executive who works with your company part-time — typically one to three days per week on a multi-month engagement — instead of joining as a full-time hire. In the specific case of a sales-and-CS rift, their job is not to run daily standups for either team. Their job is to install the connective tissue that makes the two teams operate as one revenue engine: a shared definition of a good customer, a clean handoff process, one set of numbers everyone trusts, and a compensation structure that stops rewarding the two teams for pulling in opposite directions.

The reason the misalignment exists is almost always structural rather than personal. Sales is usually compensated on new bookings and measured on quota attainment, so it optimizes for signed contracts. CS is usually measured on retention, adoption, and net revenue retention, so it optimizes for customers who succeed. When no single leader sits above both, those two incentive systems drift apart until the teams are effectively working for different companies. A fractional CRO collapses that gap by becoming — temporarily — the one person accountable for the entire number, from first touch to renewal. That is the leverage. They are not a facilitator; they are the missing apex of the org chart, rented by the day.

Because they have usually done this at several companies before yours, a good fractional CRO also brings a pre-built playbook: the lifecycle stages, the handoff checklist, the QBR cadence, the comp framework. You are not paying them to invent alignment from first principles — you are paying for the pattern recognition that lets them diagnose your specific leak in weeks rather than quarters. For a deeper look at how revenue ownership consolidates across the funnel, see the [revenue operating model overview](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revenue-operating-model).

## How do I know if my problem is actually a leadership gap or just a process gap?

This is the most important question to answer before you spend a dollar, because the fix is different for each. A process gap means the teams want to collaborate but lack the mechanics — no shared CRM fields, no defined handoff trigger, no joint account review. A leadership gap means the teams have no shared incentive or authority to collaborate at all, and would not do so even with perfect tooling. A fractional CRO is the right answer for a leadership gap. For a pure process gap, a RevOps hire or consultant is cheaper and sufficient.

Use the flow below to route your situation honestly. If you keep landing on "the teams openly blame each other" and "no single person can force a decision across both," you have a leadership gap and the fractional CRO thesis holds. If instead the teams get along but keep dropping balls, you may only need process and systems work.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Sales and CS do not talk] --> B{Is there one leader over both today}
    B -->|No| C[Leadership gap]
    B -->|Yes but overloaded| D[Capacity gap]
    A --> E{Do teams want to collaborate}
    E -->|Yes but lack tools| F[Process gap]
    E -->|No shared incentive| C
    C --> G[Fractional CRO fits well]
    D --> H[Fractional CRO or RevOps leader]
    F --> I[RevOps hire or consultant first]
```

A practical test: ask each team leader to write down, independently, what a good-fit customer looks like and who owns the account after the deal closes. If the two answers conflict, you have a leadership and definition problem, not a tooling one. No amount of Salesforce configuration fixes two teams that disagree about who they are selling to and who owns them afterward. That disagreement can only be resolved by someone with authority over both, which is precisely the seat a fractional CRO fills. The related breakdown on [sales-to-CS handoff design](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/sales-cs-handoff) covers the process-gap side in detail if that turns out to be your real issue.

## What are the signs the divide is costing you real revenue?

The gap between sales and CS is expensive, but the cost hides in metrics most founders do not watch together. The clearest signal is a widening spread between gross new bookings and net revenue retention. If sales is hitting quota while churn quietly eats the gains, the two teams are optimizing against each other and the net number is flat despite heavy activity. That pattern — strong top-line bookings, weak net retention — is the financial fingerprint of a sales-CS rift.

Other reliable tells include: onboarding times that balloon because CS inherits deals it did not scope; a rising rate of first-year churn concentrated in specific deal types, which usually means sales is closing bad-fit accounts to hit quota; expansion and upsell revenue that stays near zero because no one owns the moment when a happy customer is ready to buy more; and renewal conversations that consistently surprise the account team, which means no one is watching health signals across the lifecycle. Each of these is a symptom of the same missing owner. A fractional CRO's first deliverable is usually to quantify these leaks in dollars so you can see whether the engagement pays for itself — and in most misaligned mid-market companies, it does, several times over. The [net revenue retention primer](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/net-revenue-retention) explains why NRR is the single best number for exposing this class of problem.

If you cannot yet see these numbers because sales and CS report on separate dashboards with separate definitions, that itself is a symptom. The inability to view the full customer lifecycle in one place is both a cause and a consequence of the divide, and unifying that view is often step one of the engagement.

## What does a good fractional CRO engagement look like month by month?

A well-run engagement is time-boxed and outcome-defined, not open-ended. The classic shape is a diagnostic phase, an installation phase, and a handoff phase, typically compressed into three to six months. The goal is explicitly to make themselves unnecessary — a fractional CRO who is still indispensable at month twelve has failed at the alignment mission, because durable alignment lives in systems and incentives, not in one person's presence.

The sequence below shows the typical arc. Notice that the early weeks are about listening and measuring, the middle is about installing shared mechanics and incentives, and the final phase is about transferring ownership to your permanent leaders so the alignment outlasts the contract.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Month one diagnose] --> B[Month two align definitions]
    B --> C[Month three install handoff and comp]
    C --> D[Month four run the cadence]
    D --> E[Month five transfer ownership]
    E --> F[Month six exit or renew]
```

In month one they interview both teams, audit the pipeline and churn data, and quantify the leak. In month two they force agreement on the ideal customer profile and the definition of a qualified, well-scoped deal — the shared vocabulary both teams will use. In month three they install the concrete machinery: a handoff checklist with a hard trigger, a joint account-review cadence, and, critically, a compensation adjustment so both teams share stakes in retention and expansion, not just their own silo metric. The remaining months are about running that cadence until it is habitual, then transferring ownership to a permanent VP of Sales, Head of CS, or a full-time CRO if your scale justifies one. The [RevOps cadence and QBR guide](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revenue-cadence) details the meeting rhythm that holds this together.

The single highest-leverage change in that list is almost always the compensation fix. When you tie a slice of sales comp to net retention and a slice of CS comp to expansion, the two teams stop being able to win at each other's expense. Incentives that were pulling apart start pulling together, and much of the "they do not talk" behavior evaporates because talking is now in everyone's financial interest.

## When is a fractional CRO the wrong choice?

A fractional CRO is the wrong instrument in several clear situations, and recognizing them saves you real money. First, if you are pre-product-market-fit, your problem is not revenue alignment — it is finding something people reliably buy — and a senior revenue executive part-time will not create demand that does not yet exist. Fix PMF first. Second, if your total revenue team is tiny, say a couple of reps and one CS person, the overhead of an executive layer outweighs the benefit; you likely need a strong player-coach founder or a single RevOps hire, not a fractional C-level seat.

Third, and most common: if you are not willing to grant the fractional CRO genuine authority over both teams, do not hire one. The role only works when they can change comp plans, redraw the handoff, and overrule a team leader who resists. A fractional CRO with responsibility but no authority degrades into a well-paid mediator who writes recommendations everyone ignores. Before signing, confirm with yourself that you will let them make binding decisions — including ones your incumbent leaders dislike. Fourth, if the real problem is a specific broken system — a CRM that cannot track lifecycle stages, no product usage data reaching CS — then a RevOps or systems consultant is a cheaper, more targeted fix than an executive. Diagnose whether your gap is leadership or plumbing before you buy the leadership answer. The [when to hire RevOps vs revenue leadership](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-vs-leadership) comparison is worth reading if you are unsure which side of that line you are on.

Finally, a fractional CRO is wrong if you actually need full-time, in-the-room leadership — for example, during a hyper-growth phase where the revenue org is changing weekly and needs daily hands-on management. Fractional is built for installing systems and direction, not for high-frequency operational firefighting. Match the engagement model to the intensity your stage demands.

## How much authority and budget should I plan for?

Plan for two things: real decision authority and a defined budget with a defined outcome. On authority, write into the engagement charter that the fractional CRO owns the combined revenue number and has the power to modify comp, process, and the handoff across both teams during the engagement. Make your incumbent sales and CS leaders' cooperation an explicit expectation, communicated by you as founder or CEO before the CRO starts. Alignment fails most often not because the CRO lacks skill but because the org never truly gave them the seat.

On budget, fractional CRO engagements are priced well below a full-time executive's loaded cost precisely because they are part-time and time-boxed — that is the core economic argument for the model. The exact rate varies by market, seniority, and days per week, so get real quotes rather than trusting a rule of thumb, and always frame the cost against the quantified leak the diagnostic surfaces. If first-year churn and missing expansion are costing you a large multiple of the engagement fee, the decision is straightforward. If the leak is small, the misalignment may not yet be worth an executive intervention, and you can revisit later. The point is to make the spend decision against a measured number, not a feeling. The [revenue leadership cost framework](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revenue-leadership-cost) walks through how to model fractional versus full-time against expected recovered revenue.

Structure the contract around outcomes, not hours: define what "aligned" means in measurable terms — a documented handoff with a hard trigger, a shared ICP both teams sign, a joint cadence running for a set number of cycles, a comp plan live in both teams — and tie renewal or extension to those deliverables landing. This keeps the engagement honest and keeps the CRO focused on making themselves unnecessary rather than perpetuating the contract.

## Related questions

### Can a fractional CRO manage both sales and customer success at once?
Yes — that dual ownership is the whole point. The role exists to sit above both functions and be accountable for the combined number, which is exactly why it fixes a sales-CS divide that individual team leaders cannot resolve on their own.

### How is a fractional CRO different from a RevOps consultant?
A RevOps consultant fixes systems, data, and process plumbing. A fractional CRO owns strategy, incentives, and authority over the teams. Use RevOps for a process gap and a fractional CRO for a leadership and alignment gap.

### How long before I see results from a fractional CRO?
Expect diagnosis and quantified leaks within weeks, installed handoff and comp changes within the first few months, and measurable retention and expansion improvement over one to two renewal cycles. Alignment behavior often shifts fast once comp is fixed.

### Will hiring a fractional CRO upset my existing sales and CS leaders?
It can if handled poorly. Position the CRO as the leader who removes cross-team friction and makes both teams win, grant clear authority publicly, and involve incumbent leaders in the diagnosis so they own the fix rather than feel bypassed.

### Should I hire a full-time CRO instead?
Only if your revenue org is large and volatile enough to need daily executive presence. For installing alignment systems at mid-market scale, fractional gives you the same expertise at lower cost and with a built-in exit once the systems hold.

## FAQ

**What is a fractional CRO?**
A fractional Chief Revenue Officer is a senior revenue executive who works part-time and for a defined period, owning the full revenue number across sales, customer success, and sometimes marketing, without joining as a full-time hire.

**Does a fractional CRO replace my VP of Sales or Head of CS?**
No. They sit above both, aligning them and installing shared systems and incentives. Your team leaders keep running their functions day to day; the CRO makes those functions operate as one engine.

**How many days a week does a fractional CRO work?**
Typically one to three days per week, scaled to the intensity of the engagement. The diagnostic phase may run heavier, tapering as installed systems take over and ownership transfers to your permanent team.

**Is a fractional CRO worth it for a small company?**
It depends on the size of the revenue leak, not the size of the company. If misalignment is costing a large multiple of the fee in churn and lost expansion, it is worth it. Very small revenue teams usually need a RevOps hire first.

**What is the single most impactful change a fractional CRO makes?**
Usually the compensation fix — tying a slice of sales pay to retention and a slice of CS pay to expansion. This removes the incentive for the two teams to win at each other's expense and makes collaboration financially rational.

**How do I measure whether the engagement worked?**
Track net revenue retention, first-year churn by deal type, expansion revenue, and handoff-to-onboarding time before and after. A rising net retention number alongside stable bookings is the clearest proof the divide is closing.

**What happens when the engagement ends?**
A well-run engagement transfers ownership of the aligned systems — the shared ICP, the handoff, the cadence, the comp plan — to your permanent leaders. The alignment lives in those systems, so it should persist after the CRO exits.

**Can a fractional CRO help if we have no shared data between sales and CS?**
Yes, and unifying that view is often step one. But if the only problem is missing data plumbing, a RevOps consultant may be the cheaper starting point. A fractional CRO is warranted when the gap is leadership and incentives, not just tooling.
